extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics interested in truthful depiction of clouds and sky
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for representing clouds and skies truthfully in landscape painting, covering form, scale, light, transparency, internal structure, and compositional relationships. Emphasizes observation of natural phenomena (e.g., Turner as exemplar) and avoidance of common painterly falsehoods (e.g., repetitive pillowy forms of old masters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clouds bounded by temperature/heat-lines (decisive outlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds are not determined chiefly by wind impulses but by 'fixed lines of radiant heat' which regulate atmospheric temperature; their outlines are often steady right lines of more or less decision, sometimes exactly corresponding with the outline of the mountain on which they are formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict cloud outlines as angular and decisive where temperature boundaries dictate them (e.g., ridges, peaks mirroring mountain outline), not merely as flowing curves shaped by wind. Example/anti-pattern: representational steady right-lines vs. flowing capricious curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain overall persistence while showing internal motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Although cloud parts may be in constant rapid motion, the cloud can keep the same size, form, and place for long periods; variations are often alternate formation and disappearance of parts rather than wholesale change of position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show whirling, moving parts within a stable overall silhouette — suggest internal activity without implying the whole mass is shifting position. Avoid depicting clouds as entirely displaced by each gust of wind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angular, characterful great outlines (avoid monotony)
rubrics_metrics.description: If great lines are taken, rejecting minutiae of variation, the resultant form will almost always be angular, full of character and decision, not monotonous or uniformly convex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing the major silhouette of a cloud, prefer energetic, often angular lines and varied masses over smooth identical convex sweeps. Anti-pattern: Italian/Dutch seventeenth-century 'puffed-up' spherical repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of minor curves (varied, non-monotonous detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor contours are 'beautifully curvilinear' but never monotonous — a succession: concave, convex, an angular jag, a straight line, a curve again, a deep gap, places melted away, displaying ceaseless invention, studied inequality, delicate symmetry and contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose small-scale cloud contours with continual variation; avoid repeating the same curve type. Each fragment should read as a small 'picture' with internal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniform pillowy/cloud-bubble shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Masses composed of repeated spherical, cauliflower-like protuberances (all parts identical) are false to nature; repetition of the same rounded passages produces monotony and untruth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not copy repeated circular motifs across a cloud mass. Example/anti-pattern: Claude and Salvator's repetitive rounded sweeps; these lack individuality and are 'physically impossible' in natural cloud structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show colossal scale and retiring spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Congregated masses of cloud are vast — distances within a cloud (edge to shadow) may be miles; visible masses can be expressed in terms of miles and have mountain-like heights and ravines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray clouds with spatial depth and scale: distinct subdivisions, aerial perspective, and sense of distance. Avoid compressing large cloud-space into small, featureless rounded blobs; doing so 'banishes the variety' and robs clouds of buoyancy and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of divisions and marked aerial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and shade of clouds are invariably composed of a series of divided masses, each with outline variety; multitudinous divisions are necessary and must be sharply and forcibly marked by aerial perspective to express space and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include many internally articulated masses and use aerial perspective (changes in tone, blueness, softness) to show recession. Omitting these at large scale is 'the veriest audacity of falsehood.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, evanescence, and transmitted light (light within, not only upon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature gives evidence of transmitted sunshine even in ponderous masses; clouds have passages where vapor is visible because of light arrested within the mass, and dark sides often show opalescent and delicate hues due to beams passing through them. 'Their light is always on them, not in them' is a fault of old masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render internal translucency: allow light to pass through cloud bodies, showing opalescent hues and filmy evanescence, particularly on dark sides. Avoid making clouds solidly opaque with light only on their surface (an old-master fault).

rubrics_metrics.name: Edges: melting, breaking, and invisible margins
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud edges are often broken, invisible, or only felt when the eye is not fixed; edges may be darker than centers where light penetrates at the edge and passes through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model edges variably: some edges should melt into atmosphere, others be sharply outlined or even darker than interior due to transmitted light effects. Use broken outlines and delicate modulation to suggest distance and filmy texture. Example: Turner's edges that are 'first invisible, then all but imaginary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of infinity and avoidance of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'expression of infinity' — perpetual variation with no repetition — is a near-unerring test of truth in painting. What is not infinite cannot be true; repetition is evidence the artist has not 'gone to nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for continual, unrepeatable variety in forms and details across the painted sky. Do not think that multiplying objects or enlarging size creates infinity; mere number or bulk without true variation is a novice's resource and still false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use associations of cloud-types (cirrostratus with cumulus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low horizontal bars or fields of cloud (cirrostratus) frequently associate with cumulus—capping or floating on its flanks—opposing the rolling cumulus and giving apparent solidity and vastness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include natural associations (e.g., horizontal cirrostratus flakes with cumulus) to enhance the impression of scale and to create compositional opposition; this natural composition often surpasses contrived invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision and articulation of light and shadow (chiaroscuro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both light and shade in cloud masses are composed of multitudinous divided masses, with broken irregular shadow and transparency; the lowest cumuli produce 'breaking irregular shadow and transparency' rather than a single flat dark side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate shadows as composed masses with internal modulation; avoid flat half-light/half-dark depictions. Use delicate shadow modulation to suggest depth and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and incorporate refined, rare natural truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain phenomena (e.g., a pale wreath of parallel cloud repeating a snowy mountain outline) are subtle and require intimate, scientific familiarity with particular landscapes to perceive and render.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study specific atmospheric phenomena in situ and incorporate refined observations into work where appropriate — even small, rarely-noticed truths can testify to the artist's knowledge and give authenticity to a picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey buoyancy, elasticity, and inward energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds in perfect repose can 'boil, rise, and melt' with buoyancy and elasticity of inward energy indicated even through ponderous forms; great masses may show sharp cutting edges and dark outlines where forms project against light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render a sense of internal life — buoyant, elastic motion — within even heavy cloud masses. Use bold outlines where appropriate to suggest forms without losing breadth; Turner's use of such outlines gives solidity and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw clouds structurally (use of drawing/media beyond mere brush-wash)
rubrics_metrics.description: True drawing of cloud-form requires articulation of chiaroscuro and structural understanding, not merely leaving white paper or light washes. Many painters treat clouds as dependent on brush and wash alone and therefore fail to understand their anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice drawing clouds (chalk, lead, or similar) to learn form before rendering with brush; aim for structure, parts, and solidity rather than relying on clever washes or erased shapes. Example: Stanfield praised for 'chiselled' cloud-form; many moderns fail when they attempt detail with brush alone.
